content: The updated guidelines focus on the care and treatment of individuals diagnosed with chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. These updates revise the care and treatment recommendations from the 2016 WHO guidelines and incorporate new evidence and approaches for managing HCV. In 2017, the WHO guidelines on hepatitis B and C testing were updated to refine the screening recommendations. These guidelines are intended for use by government officials, national program managers, and healthcare providers, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, to develop policies, plans, and treatment protocols for hepatitis care. The WHO developed these guidelines following its Guidelines Review Committee procedures. Systematic reviews were conducted to evaluate the safety and efficacy of treatment regimens in adults, assess morbidity and mortality from extrahepatic manifestations of HCV, and review cost-effectiveness literature. Additionally, modeling was performed to support the recommendations. A multidisciplinary Guidelines Development Group convened in September 2017 to formulate recommendations using the GRADE approach, which considers the quality of evidence, the balance of benefits and harms, patient and healthcare worker preferences, resource use, cost-effectiveness, and feasibility in resource-limited settings. Key Recommendations: 1. When to Start Treatment: Treatment is recommended for all individuals aged 12 years or older diagnosed with HCV infection, regardless of disease stage, except for pregnant women. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. 2. Treatment Regimens for Adults and Adolescents: Pangenotypic regimens, defined as those achieving a sustained virological response (SVR) rate of over 85% across all six major HCV genotypes, are recommended. For individuals with HCV genotype 3 infection who have previously received interferon and/or ribavirin, a 16-week treatment course is advised (conditional recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). For adolescents aged 12–17 years or weighing at least 35 kg with chronic HCV infection: Sofosbuvir/ledipasvir for 12 weeks for genotypes 1, 4, 5, and 6. Sofosbuvir/ribavirin for 12 weeks for genotype 2. Sofosbuvir/ribavirin for 24 weeks for genotype 3 (strong recommendation, very low-quality evidence). 3. Pangenotypic Regimens for Adults: For adults without cirrhosis: Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for 12 weeks. Sofosbuvir/daclatasvir for 12 weeks. Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir for 8 weeks. For adults with compensated cirrhosis: Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for 12 weeks. Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir for 12 weeks. Sofosbuvir/daclatasvir for 24 weeks (or 12 weeks in specific cases). 4. Treatment for Children Under 12 Years: Treatment should be deferred until the child reaches 12 years of age (conditional recommendation, very low-quality evidence). Interferon-based regimens should no longer be used (strong recommendation, very low-quality evidence). 5. Clinical Considerations: Pangenotypic regimens eliminate the need for genotyping before treatment initiation. Non-invasive tests like APRI or FIB-4 can be used to assess liver fibrosis and cirrhosis in resource-limited settings. Direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) are well-tolerated with minimal side effects, reducing the need for frequent laboratory monitoring. SVR at 12 weeks post-treatment is used to determine treatment success. 6. Special Populations: HIV/HCV Coinfection: Individuals with HIV/HCV coinfection are at higher risk for fibrosis progression and should be prioritized for treatment. Drug-drug interactions with antiretroviral medications must be considered. HBV/HCV Coinfection: HBV reactivation can occur during HCV treatment. HBV treatment eligibility should be assessed, and treatment initiated if necessary to prevent reactivation. Cirrhosis: Individuals with cirrhosis, even after achieving SVR, should undergo regular screening for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Chronic Kidney Disease: Data on sofosbuvir-based regimens in individuals with severe renal impairment are limited. Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir is effective for all six major genotypes in patients with chronic kidney disease. TB/HCV Coinfection: Active tuberculosis treatment should precede HCV treatment. TB/HCV coinfected individuals are at increased risk of hepatotoxicity. 7. Retreatment After DAA Failure: Currently, sofosbuvir/velpatasvir/voxilaprevir is the only approved pangenotypic DAA regimen for retreatment after prior DAA failure. Investigations into treatment failure should include adherence assessment and evaluation of potential drug-drug interactions. 8. Simplified Service Delivery Models: An eight-point approach supports the implementation of clinical recommendations, including comprehensive national planning, standardized care algorithms, integration of hepatitis services, strategies to strengthen linkage to care, decentralized services, community engagement, efficient procurement, and data systems to monitor care quality. 9. Public Health Considerations: Specific population groups, such as people who inject drugs, individuals in prisons, men who have sex with men, sex workers, and indigenous populations, require tailored public health approaches due to high incidence, stigma, discrimination, and barriers to accessing services. 10. HCV Testing Recommendations: Focused testing in high-risk populations and general population testing in settings with ≥2% or ≥5% HCV antibody seroprevalence are recommended. Birth cohort testing may be applied to older individuals at higher risk of infection and morbidity. 11. Testing and Monitoring: HCV infection in children under 18 months can only be confirmed using virological assays due to the presence of maternal antibodies. Serological assays (antibody or antibody/antigen) are recommended for initial testing, followed by nucleic acid testing (NAT) for confirmation of viraemic infection. HCV core antigen testing is an alternative to NAT in resource-limited settings. 12. Alcohol Use and Liver Fibrosis Assessment: Alcohol intake assessment and behavioral interventions to reduce alcohol consumption are recommended for individuals with HCV infection. APRI or FIB-4 tests are suggested for liver fibrosis assessment in resource-limited settings. These updated guidelines aim to provide evidence-based recommendations for the diagnosis, treatment, and monitoring of chronic HCV infection in children, adolescents, and adults, with a focus on improving access to care and treatment in resource-limited settings.
